chapters.caption: St Mary's from Radcliffe Square — the church at the very centre of the university's story.
chapters.directions: Enter through the main door from the High Street (or the Radcliffe Square side) and pause just inside the nave.
chapters.text: Every university has a beginning, and Oxford's begins in this church. Long before there were colleges with their gates and quadrangles, there were masters and students meeting here, at St Mary the Virgin on the High Street — the university's first home, its first library, its parliament and its church all in one. The university quite literally grew up around this building: teaching began in and around St Mary's in the 1100s, the earliest university library was kept upstairs here, and the congregation of the whole university met in this nave. The church you see today is a glorious layer cake. The tower is the oldest part, built around 1280 and crowned a generation later, between 1315 and 1325, with one of the most beautiful spires in England — look for the statues of saints sheltering under little gabled canopies at its corners. The body of the church is mostly 15th and early 16th century, rebuilt as Oxford grew rich. And stuck on the front, as we'll see, is a flamboyant Baroque porch that nearly cost an archbishop his head — well, it was Exhibit A at his trial, and he lost his head in the end. This is still a working parish church and the official church of the university, so you may find a service, a rehearsal or a sermon in progress. That's not an interruption; it's the building doing, today, exactly what it has done for 800 years.
chapters.title: The Church Where the University Began

chapters.caption: The bright Perpendicular nave — the university's meeting place, debating hall and courtroom.
chapters.directions: Walk slowly up the centre aisle toward the chancel, then look back at the west end before exploring the side chapels.
chapters.text: Stand in the middle of the nave and soak it in. For a medieval church, St Mary's is surprisingly bright and open — the Victorians would have darkened it, but here the big Perpendicular windows still pour in light, and the space feels less like a fortress of faith and more like a great civic hall. That's because it was one. This nave hosted the university's Congregation, its governing assembly; degrees were conferred here, disputes settled here, sermons preached here that changed English religion. John Wesley preached from this pulpit in the 1740s. In 1833 John Keble preached the sermon here that launched the Oxford Movement, and John Henry Newman — later Cardinal Newman — was the vicar of this church from 1828 to 1843, preaching sermons people crossed the city to hear. In 1941, C. S. Lewis stood here and delivered 'The Weight of Glory,' one of the most famous sermons of the 20th century. Look up at the roof and along the walls for the monuments of university men stacked through the centuries. Then look down and find the pillar with the odd notch hacked out of it — hold that thought; it's the key to the church's darkest story, coming in a couple of chapters. First, the chancel at the east end: the oldest worshipping space in the building, quieter and more intimate, where university sermons are still preached in term time.
chapters.title: The Nave and Chancel: Oxford's Original Lecture Hall

chapters.caption: The Virgin Porch of 1637 — Baroque exuberance that became evidence at an archbishop's trial.
chapters.directions: Head back toward the tower end of the church to find the Adam de Brome Chapel on the north side.
chapters.text: Before the chapels, nip outside to the High Street front and look at the porch, because it's one of the great characters of Oxford architecture. The Virgin Porch was built in 1637, a swirl of Baroque spirals and shells crowned by a statue of the Virgin and Child, designed in the workshop of Nicholas Stone. In sober post-Reformation England, this was a provocatively Catholic-looking flourish — and when Archbishop William Laud, the university's chancellor, came to trial in 1641, his Puritan enemies literally listed this porch and its statue among the charges against him. Laud was executed in 1645. Look closely at the statue and the stonework around the door: local legend — and the pockmarks support it — says Cromwell's soldiers used the Virgin for target practice during the Civil War. Now come back inside and find the Adam de Brome Chapel, on the north side of the church. Adam de Brome was a royal chaplain who in 1326 founded Oriel College, and this chapel, built in his lifetime, carries his name and his tomb. But its real claim to fame is upstairs: the room above this chapel area held the university's first library in the 14th century, a single room of chained books that is the direct ancestor of the mighty Bodleian you've just visited. Everything in Oxford, you begin to notice, starts in a very small room.
chapters.title: The Adam de Brome Chapel and the Virgin Porch

chapters.caption: The Martyrs' Memorial (1841–43), at the north end of St Giles, honouring Latimer, Ridley and Cranmer.
chapters.directions: Return to the nave and find the entrance to the tower — tickets are sold in the church shop.
chapters.text: Now for that notch in the pillar. In 1555, under the Catholic Queen Mary, three of England's leading Protestant churchmen — Hugh Latimer, Bishop of Worcester; Nicholas Ridley, Bishop of London; and Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury — were brought to this church to be tried for heresy. They had already been imprisoned for two years, some of it in the Bocardo prison by the North Gate. The trials were staged here in the nave, packed with university men, and the outcome was never really in doubt. Latimer and Ridley were burned at the stake on Broad Street on 16 October 1555 — Latimer's famous words to Ridley, as the flames were lit, promised that they would that day 'light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out.' Cranmer's end was stranger and more dramatic. Broken by months of pressure, he signed recantations of his Protestant beliefs — then, brought here to St Mary's in March 1556 to make his submission public, he stood on a wooden platform fixed to that notched pillar, renounced his recantations, denounced the Pope, and promised that the hand which had signed them would burn first. Hours later he kept that promise at the stake, holding his right hand into the flame. A cobbled cross in Broad Street marks the spot, and the tall Martyrs' Memorial at the end of St Giles, raised in the 1840s, keeps the story in the city's skyline. Stand by the pillar for a moment. Few stones in Oxford have seen a braver speech.
chapters.title: The Trial of the Oxford Martyrs

chapters.caption: The view from the tower: the Radcliffe Camera below, with All Souls and the dreaming spires beyond.
chapters.directions: Descend carefully — you'll come down the same way you went up — and exit into Radcliffe Square.
chapters.text: Time to earn the best view in Oxford. The tower is the oldest part of the church, raised around 1280, and climbing it is a small adventure in itself: 127 worn stone steps up a tight spiral staircase, past the clock room, squeezing through passages built for slimmer, shorter centuries. Take your time, mind your head, and leave big backpacks below — the stair genuinely is that narrow. Then you step out onto the parapet, 128 feet up, and Oxford arranges itself around you like a model. This is the famous 'dreaming spires' panorama, and from here you can finally understand the city's layout. Directly below, the great round dome of the Radcliffe Camera fills Radcliffe Square. Beyond it, the Old Bodleian and the pinnacles of Exeter and Jesus Colleges; to the east, the twin towers of All Souls and the long roof of the Queen's College; to the west, the whole spire-crowded skyline marching toward the castle mound. Look for the green copper dome of the Sackler Library, the Saxon tower of St Michael at the North Gate — older than the university itself — and, on a clear day, the hills that cup the city. Up here you also get the tower's own details at touching distance: the gargoyles, the pinnacles, and the statues of saints that have weathered seven centuries of Oxford rain. On the way down, spare a thought for the ringers — this tower still has a working ring of bells, hauled up those same stairs, in pieces, by hand.
chapters.title: The Tower Climb: The Best View in Oxford

chapters.caption: The Radcliffe Camera (1737–49) by James Gibbs — England's first circular library, now a Bodleian reading room.
chapters.directions: Walk clockwise around the square: All Souls is on the east side, Brasenose on the west.
chapters.text: Back at ground level, give the square's centrepiece its moment. The Radcliffe Camera is Oxford's icon — the building on the postcards, the jigsaws, the university's own logo-like shorthand — and it began with a doctor's fortune. John Radcliffe, physician to William III and Queen Anne and the richest medic of his age, died in 1714 leaving £40,000 to build a library in Oxford. It took time to clear the houses, gardens and a brewery that stood on this site, but between 1737 and 1749 the architect James Gibbs raised something England had never seen: a free-standing circular library, a great rusticated drum ringed with paired Corinthian columns and capped with a lead dome. It opened on 13 April 1749 as the Radcliffe Science Library — 'camera' is simply Latin for a room or chamber. The science books eventually moved out to the new university museum quarter, and in 1861 the Camera became what it remains today: a reading room of the Bodleian Library, linked to the Old Library by an underground tunnel and book store burrowed beneath the square you're standing on. That means, sadly, that it's not open to casual visitors — the students you see slipping in with their university cards are going to work, mostly in the history collections. But honestly, the Camera gives its best to the street: circle it slowly, watch the dome change with the light, and note how Gibbs made a round building sit perfectly happily among Gothic neighbours.
chapters.title: Radcliffe Square and the Radcliffe Camera

chapters.caption: All Souls College from the square — a college of fellows only, famous for the hardest examination in Oxford lore.
chapters.directions: Complete the circuit of the square back to the church, or slip down Brasenose Lane toward the High Street.
chapters.text: Two great colleges frame the square, and both reward a slow look from the outside. On the east side stands All Souls, founded in 1438 by Archbishop Henry Chichele as a college of prayer and study for the souls of the English dead of the Hundred Years' War — hence the name. It is unlike any other Oxford college: it has no undergraduates at all. Its members are fellows — established scholars and a handful of brilliant recent graduates who win places through a fellowship examination long mythologised as the hardest exam in the country, the one whose essay paper once asked candidates to write on a single word. From the square, admire its twin-towered Gothic front, designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor in the early 1700s — deliberately medieval-looking in an age of classical taste, to match the older chapel beside it. Behind those walls lie the Codrington Library and one of Christopher Wren's finest sundials. Across the square to the west is Brasenose College, founded in 1509, whose name comes from a 'brazen nose' — a brass door-knocker shaped like a nose that once adorned its hall door. The original knocker spent centuries in Stamford, in Lincolnshire, after students fled there in a medieval riot; the college finally got it back in 1890, and it now hangs in the dining hall, guarded like treasure. Brasenose's mellow frontage completes the square's west side, and its students get to wake up to the Camera view every single morning — not a bad start to a degree.
chapters.title: All Souls and Brasenose: The Square's Bookends

chapters.caption: Brasenose College, founded 1509 — named for its brazen-nose door knocker, finally returned in 1890.
chapters.directions: Radcliffe Square connects north to Broad Street (for the Weston Library and Sheldonian) and south to the High Street.
chapters.text: Let's finish where we started, in the middle of the square, with the whole composition around you: church, library, camera and colleges, six centuries of architecture holding a conversation across the cobbles. If you take one idea away from St Mary's, make it this: Oxford did not begin with colleges at all. It began with a church, a handful of masters, and students lodging in halls around the High Street — and this building watched every later chapter arrive: the first library upstairs, the martyrs in the nave, Wesley and Newman in the pulpit, and today's visitors panting happily down its tower stairs. Before you move on, the church's own Vaults and Garden café, tucked into the old Congregation House on the north side, is one of the nicest coffee stops in the centre — vaulted stone above, garden behind, and a menu with a conscience. The church shop, too, is better than most. If the tower queue put you off earlier, check it again now; late afternoon light on the spires is the finest of the day, and the climb is the single best orientation you can give yourself in Oxford. From here, Broad Street and the Weston Library are two minutes north, the High Street's colleges stretch east, and King's Arms and the covered market call from the west. Wherever you go next in this city, you'll be walking in the parish of St Mary's — for most of Oxford's history, there wasn't anywhere else.
chapters.title: Wrap-Up: Standing at the Centre of It All

intro: If Oxford has a centre of gravity, this is it. The University Church of St Mary the Virgin is where the university began — its first library, its first great assembly, and the stage for some of the most dramatic scenes in English history, including the trial of the Oxford Martyrs. Around it spreads Radcliffe Square, the most beautiful enclosed space in the city, ringed by the Radcliffe Camera, All Souls and Brasenose. This tour takes you through the church, up its medieval tower for the definitive Oxford view, and then around the square to read the buildings from the outside. Allow about an hour, plus queuing time for the tower on busy days.

location.name: University Church of St Mary the Virgin, High Street, Oxford

mapNote: The church stands on the south side of Radcliffe Square, with its main entrance on the High Street. Start inside the church (nave, chapels, martyrs' pillar), then climb the tower — the entrance is inside the church, by the shop. Afterwards, walk the square clockwise: Radcliffe Camera in the centre, All Souls to the east, Brasenose to the west, the Bodleian to the north. Everything in this tour is within a 200-metre circle.
practical: Admission to the church is free; the tower climb is ticketed and bought at the church shop — go early or late in the day to beat the queue.
The tower has 127 narrow, steep spiral steps and no lift; it's unsuitable for anyone with mobility or claustrophobia issues, and large bags can't be taken up.
The church is a working parish church: it may close to visitors during services, weddings and university sermons, especially on Sundays.
The cobbled cross set into Broad Street, a short walk west, marks the spot where the Oxford Martyrs were burned; the Martyrs' Memorial stands at the north end of St Giles.
The Vaults and Garden café, in the church's old Congregation House, serves breakfast, lunch and coffee with a garden behind.
Radcliffe Camera is a working reading room and is not open to the public; enjoy it from the square and from the tower above.
subtitle: Where the university began — martyrs, a Baroque porch, and the finest view in Oxford
